properties.decision:
RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING, NOT AS A PROPOSAL. Nothing here is intent. Anthony, 2026-08-11: "since every reflow2 project will use git repo, then a project needs to shape its own governance rules for that project."

⭐ THE ARGUMENT IS UNIVERSALITY, AND IT IS WHAT MAKES THIS A PRODUCT QUESTION RATHER THAN REPO HYGIENE. `req:persistence` is ACCEPTED — the design lives in-repo alongside the code — so a git repository is not one deployment choice among many, it is the substrate every reflow2 project stands on. That makes the QUESTIONS predictable even though the ANSWERS are not: who may merge, what may land on the main line, when the design export is written, whether breaking any of it should stop a build. Every project will face them; each will answer differently.

WHAT ALREADY EXISTS, and the gap is in the TRIGGER rather than the vocabulary:
  · `cap:governance-proposal` — BUILT and shipping. Asks what breaking a rule should cost and writes
    `enforced` explicitly in both directions. But it is REACTIVE: it fires when somebody happens to
    state a rule. Nothing asks the question first.
  · `DesignRule` + three-state `enforced` + `unverified_enforced_rule` — the layer is there.
  · `req:a-project-records-how-it-ships` (proposed, Anthony 2026-07-31) — ADJACENT AND NOT THE SAME.
    That is the ordered RELEASE PROCEDURE, and its own text says the steps are not derivable from
    the graph. This is workflow AUTHORITY and TIMING, which is a different question with the same
    property: not derivable, project-specific, and currently unrecorded until someone volunteers it.
  · `genesis` captures deployment and platform context as Requirements — target platforms, the
    driving agent — and captures NOTHING about how the project's work reaches its main line.
  · `req:a-node-can-say-who-may-change-it` (proposed) — node-level authority, not merge authority.

📌 AND HIS OWN 2026-08-08 FRAMING ALREADY NAMED MERGING, in the entry that produced reflow2's governance layer: "every project will be managed differently and have differing sets of people running it with their own practices and POLICIES ABOUT MERGING AND WHO CAN MERGE and other governing mechanisms — but allowing reflow2 to setup a generic set of nodes/edges that allow a user or set of users to define their own project management policies/governance in graph form is something that I think would be really helpful." The capture half of that shipped. The half that would make a project actually reach for it did not.

⭐ WHY REACTIVE CAPTURE IS NOT ENOUGH, measured rather than argued. reflow2 itself has run for weeks with `rule:nothing-lands-on-main-directly` stated NOWHERE in its design until 2026-08-09 — that rule's own text records it: "it lived in an agent's memory file and in Anthony's head, and it was followed twice that day by a session reading it from neither." A reactive mechanism cannot capture a rule nobody thinks to state, and a rule everybody follows is exactly the one nobody states.

IDEAS, unranked:
(a) ASK AT GENESIS/ADOPT. A short set of workflow questions alongside the deployment ones, each landing as a DesignRule with its consequence stated. Reaches every project once, at the moment the repo is being set up anyway.
(b) ASK WHEN THE EVIDENCE APPEARS, not at bootstrap. A design that has gained a Release, or a second Contributor, or a second seat, has demonstrably reached the point where merge authority matters — and at genesis nobody has an opinion yet, which is the same objection that makes asking for feedback consent at INSTALL read worse than at UPDATE.
(c) SHIP A STARTER SET as advisory DesignRules the project edits or deletes — reflow2's own four, generalised. Fastest to value and the most dangerous: a default rule is an opinion nobody chose, which is precisely what `cap:governance-proposal` exists to prevent, and `req:defaults-do-not-assert` forbids.
(d) Nothing. The vocabulary is there; a project that wants governance can state it, and prompting risks manufacturing policy nobody needed.

⚠️ THE STRONGEST OBJECTION, and it is Anthony's own from a different day: `dec:proposed-requirements-pruned` dropped two requirements as "backlog hygiene dressed as product requirements", with the test being whether a requirement changes what anyone BUILDS. A prompt that produces four DesignRules nobody enforces has changed nothing and added four nodes. What would save (a) or (b) from that is the CONSEQUENCE question — governance-proposal's actual contribution — because a rule with a stated, chosen consequence does change what the build does.

⚠️ SECOND: the questions are only universal if they stay in PURE GIT. "Who may merge" is a forge concept on GitHub and a filesystem-permission concept on a bare remote; "what lands on the main line" is expressible in plain git and survives both. See dec:idea-should-reflow2-carry-its-own-git-discipline, where reflow2's own rule is stated entirely in GitHub's vocabulary and is partly unfollowable without one.

⚠️ THIRD, the scale objection: a solo project and a seven-session fleet need different answers, and asking a solo developer to state merge authority is asking him to gate himself — which is exactly why Anthony made reflow2's own branch-then-PR rule ADVISORY rather than enforced ("there is nobody to stop"). Any prompt must be able to accept "nobody, it is just me" as a real answer rather than an incomplete one.
properties.name: OPEN — every reflow2 project uses a git repo, so should reflow2 PROMPT each one to shape its own workflow governance rather than wait for someone to state them?
properties.rationale: Git is the substrate every reflow2 project stands on, which makes the governance questions predictable even though the answers differ per project. The capture half shipped and is reactive; nothing asks first. reflow2's own experience is the evidence that reactive is insufficient — its branch-then-PR rule existed nowhere in its design for weeks while being followed daily, because a rule everybody follows is the one nobody thinks to state.
